blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Unit 10 (Solution of Trigonometric Equations), arranged by the unit's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each one is solved briefly, step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define a trigonometric equation and give two examples.
blocks.explanation: A trigonometric equation is an equation that involves one or more trigonometric functions (or their inverses), e.g. \(2\cos x = 1\) and \(\tan^{2}x - 3 = 0\).

book_ref.quote: A trigonometric equation is an equation that involves one or more trigonometric functions

blocks.prompt: 2 Define the principal solutions and the general solution of a trigonometric equation.
blocks.explanation: The solutions in the interval \([0, 2\pi]\) are the principal solutions. Adding or subtracting multiples of the period to them gives all solutions, called the general solution (written with \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\)).

book_ref.quote: adding or subtracting multiples of the period generates all possible solutions called the general solution

blocks.prompt: 3 Solve \(\tan x = -1\).
blocks.explanation: Reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\); \(\tan\) is negative in II and IV: \(x = \pi - \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{3\pi}{4}\), \(x = 2\pi - \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{7\pi}{4}\). Period \(\pi\): general solution \(x = \frac{3\pi}{4} + n\pi\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

book_ref.quote: Reference angle from the positive value, quadrants from the sign

blocks.prompt: 4 Solve \(2\cos x - \sqrt{3} = 0\).
blocks.explanation: \(\cos x = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\); reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\); I and IV: \(x = \frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{11\pi}{6}\). General solution \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{6} + 2n\pi\right\} \cup \left\{\frac{11\pi}{6} + 2n\pi\right\}\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

book_ref.quote: Since cosine is positive, so \(x\) lies in the I and IV quadrant

blocks.prompt: 5 Solve \(\sqrt{3}\cot x + 1 = 0\).
blocks.explanation: \(\cot x = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \Rightarrow \tan x = -\sqrt{3}\); reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\); II and IV: \(x = \frac{2\pi}{3}, \frac{5\pi}{3}\). Period \(\pi\): \(x = \frac{2\pi}{3} + n\pi\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

book_ref.quote: Period \(2\pi\) for \(\sin\), \(\cos\), \(\sec\), \(\csc\); period \(\pi\) for \(\tan\), \(\cot\)

blocks.prompt: 6 Solve \(\sec x = \sqrt{2}\).
blocks.explanation: \(\cos x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\); reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\); I and IV: \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{7\pi}{4}\). General solution \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{4} + 2n\pi\right\} \cup \left\{\frac{7\pi}{4} + 2n\pi\right\}\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

book_ref.quote: \(\cos x = \frac{1}{\sec x}\), and the reciprocal of

blocks.prompt: 7 Solve \(\csc x = -2\).
blocks.explanation: \(\sin x = -\frac{1}{2}\); reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\); III and IV: \(x = \pi + \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{7\pi}{6}\), \(x = 2\pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{11\pi}{6}\). General solution \(\left\{\frac{7\pi}{6} + 2n\pi\right\} \cup \left\{\frac{11\pi}{6} + 2n\pi\right\}\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

book_ref.quote: Since sine is negative, \(x\) lies in the III and IV quadrants with reference angle

blocks.prompt: 8 Write the general solution of (i) \(\sin x = 0\) (ii) \(\cos x = 1\) (iii) \(\cos x = -1\).
blocks.explanation: (i) \(x = n\pi\) (ii) \(x = 2n\pi\) (iii) \(x = \pi + 2n\pi\), with \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\) in each case.

book_ref.quote: Special values with no quadrant pair

blocks.explanation: Isolate the square, take both signs, then solve each basic equation.

book_ref.quote: After \(\pm\) (square roots) solve both cases; the general solution is the union of all families.

blocks.explanation: Change to sine, keep both signs of the square root.

book_ref.quote: Taking the reference angle from a negative number

blocks.final_answer: Principal solutions \(\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{3\pi}{4}, \frac{5\pi}{4}, \frac{7\pi}{4}\); general solution \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{4} + n\pi\right\} \cup \left\{\frac{3\pi}{4} + n\pi\right\}\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\)

blocks.explanation: Factorise as a quadratic in \(\sin x\).

book_ref.quote: a product is zero only when one of its factors is zero

blocks.prompt: 12 Solve \(2\cos^{2}x + \sin x - 1 = 0\).
blocks.explanation: Use \(\cos^{2}x = 1 - \sin^{2}x\) to get a quadratic in \(\sin x\).

book_ref.quote: Reduce the equation to one or more basic equations

blocks.prompt: 13 Solve \(\sin x\cos x = \cos x\).
blocks.explanation: \(\cos x(\sin x - 1) = 0\). \(\cos x = 0\): \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}\); \(\sin x = 1\): \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\) (already found). So \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}\); general solution \(x = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\). (Cancelling \(\cos x\) would lose \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\).)

book_ref.quote: We do not cancel \(\cos x\); cancelling would lose the case \(\cos x = 0\).

blocks.prompt: 14 Solve \(2\cos^{2}x - \sqrt{3}\cos x = 0\).
blocks.explanation: \(\cos x(2\cos x - \sqrt{3}) = 0\). \(\cos x = 0\): \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}\); \(\cos x = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\): \(x = \frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{11\pi}{6}\). General solution \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi\right\} \cup \left\{\frac{\pi}{6} + 2n\pi\right\} \cup \left\{\frac{11\pi}{6} + 2n\pi\right\}\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

book_ref.quote: never cancel a factor that contains \(x\)

blocks.prompt: 15 Solve \(\tan x + \cot x = 2\).
blocks.explanation: Write \(\cot x = \frac{1}{\tan x}\) and clear the fraction.

book_ref.quote: If you squared, multiplied by a variable expression, or the equation has \(\tan\), \(\cot\), \(\sec\), \(\csc\), put every root back into the original equation.

blocks.prompt: 16 Solve \(\sin 2x = \frac{1}{2}\).
blocks.explanation: Solve for \(2x\) first with period \(2\pi\), then divide by 2.

book_ref.quote: \(\sin x = k\), \(\cos x = k\) or \(\tan x = k\) (use identities, factorise; never cancel

blocks.prompt: 17 Why must every root be checked after squaring both sides of a trigonometric equation?
blocks.explanation: If \(A^{2} = B^{2}\) then \(A = B\) or \(A = -B\). Squaring \(A = B\) therefore also solves \(A = -B\), and its roots (extraneous roots) do not satisfy the original equation. Substituting each root in the original equation removes them.

blocks.prompt: 18 Show that \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{4} + 2n\pi\right\} \cup \left\{\frac{3\pi}{4} + 2n\pi\right\} \cup \left\{\frac{5\pi}{4} + 2n\pi\right\} \cup \left\{\frac{7\pi}{4} + 2n\pi\right\}\) can be written as \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{4} + n\pi\right\} \cup \left\{\frac{3\pi}{4} + n\pi\right\}\).
blocks.explanation: \(\frac{5\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{4} + \pi\) and \(\frac{7\pi}{4} = \frac{3\pi}{4} + \pi\). So \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{4} + 2n\pi\right\} \cup \left\{\frac{5\pi}{4} + 2n\pi\right\}\) is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) plus every even and every odd multiple of \(\pi\), i.e. \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{4} + n\pi\right\}\); in the same way the other two give \(\left\{\frac{3\pi}{4} + n\pi\right\}\).

book_ref.quote: the book's form with four sets is the safer one

blocks.prompt: 19 Find all solutions of \(\sin x = \frac{1}{2}\) in the interval \([-2\pi, 2\pi]\).
blocks.explanation: General solution \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{6} + 2n\pi\right\} \cup \left\{\frac{5\pi}{6} + 2n\pi\right\}\). \(n = 0\): \(\frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{5\pi}{6}\); \(n = -1\): \(-\frac{11\pi}{6}, -\frac{7\pi}{6}\). So \(x = -\frac{11\pi}{6}, -\frac{7\pi}{6}, \frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{5\pi}{6}\).

book_ref.quote: For \(n = 1\) we get \(\frac{\pi}{3} + 2\pi = \frac{7\pi}{3}\)

blocks.prompt: 20 Describe the graphical method of solving \(f(x) = g(x)\).
blocks.explanation: Plot \(y = f(x)\) and \(y = g(x)\) on the same axes with the same scale. Each point where the curves intersect gives a solution: its \(x\)-coordinate satisfies \(f(x) = g(x)\).

book_ref.quote: plotting the graphs of both sides of the equation and identifying their points of intersection

blocks.prompt: 21 Why is \(x\) measured in radians when \(\cos x = \frac{x}{3}\) is solved graphically?
blocks.explanation: \(x\) appears outside the cosine too, in \(\frac{x}{3}\). This makes sense only when the angle is a real number, i.e. in radians; in degrees the line and the curve would be on different scales.

book_ref.quote: Always measure \(x\) in radians

blocks.prompt: 22 Find the interval that contains all real solutions of \(\sin x = \frac{x}{6}\).
blocks.explanation: \(-1 \le \sin x \le 1 \Rightarrow -1 \le \frac{x}{6} \le 1 \Rightarrow -6 \le x \le 6\). All solutions lie in \([-6, 6]\).

book_ref.quote: If no interval is given, use the range of the trigonometric side

blocks.prompt: 23 Use the sign test to show that \(\cos x = x\) has a root between \(0\) and \(1\).
blocks.explanation: Let \(f(x) = \cos x - x\). \(f(0) = 1 > 0\) and \(f(1) = \cos 1 - 1 \approx 0.5403 - 1 = -0.4597 < 0\). The sign changes, so the graphs of \(y = \cos x\) and \(y = x\) cross between \(0\) and \(1\).

book_ref.quote: To improve a reading, use the sign test

blocks.prompt: 24 How many real solutions does \(\sin x = \frac{x}{3}\) have? Give reasons.
blocks.explanation: Limit the interval with the range of sine, count crossings for x > 0, then use symmetry.

book_ref.quote: Use symmetry (odd functions) and periodicity

steps: At \(\frac{\pi}{2}\): \(1 > 0.52\); at \(3\): \(\sin 3 \approx 0.14 < 1\). The curve falls and the line rises on \(\left[\frac{\pi}{2}, 3\right]\): exactly one crossing (\(x \approx 2.28\)); on \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) the curve stays above the line
Both sides are odd functions, so \(x \approx -2.28\) is also a solution

blocks.prompt: 25 Show that \(x = 0\) is not a solution of \(\cos x = \frac{x}{5}\).
blocks.explanation: At \(x = 0\): \(\cos 0 = 1\) but \(\frac{0}{5} = 0\). Since \(1 \ne 0\), the two graphs do not meet at \(x = 0\) (only the line passes through the origin).

book_ref.quote: Counting a point where only one graph passes

blocks.prompt: 26 Write the vertical asymptotes of \(y = \tan x\) in \([-\pi, \pi]\) and say why they cannot be solutions of \(\tan x = \frac{x}{4}\).
blocks.explanation: \(\cos x = 0\) at \(x = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}\), so the asymptotes are \(x = -\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\). There \(\tan x\) is not defined, so these values cannot satisfy the equation.

book_ref.quote: always draw the asymptotes first as dashed lines

blocks.prompt: 27 Between which values does \(y = 2\cos x + 1\) move? Give its values at \(x = 0, \frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\).
blocks.explanation: \(2\cos x\) lies between \(-2\) and \(2\); adding \(1\) gives \(-1 \le y \le 3\). At \(x = 0, \frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\): \(y = 3, 1, -1\).

book_ref.quote: the number in front stretches the wave vertically (amplitude)

blocks.prompt: 28 A graph shows a root of \(\sin x = \frac{x}{3}\) near \(2.25\). Show that the root lies between \(2.2\) and \(2.3\).
blocks.explanation: Let \(f(x) = \sin x - \frac{x}{3}\). \(f(2.2) \approx 0.8085 - 0.7333 = 0.0752 > 0\); \(f(2.3) \approx 0.7457 - 0.7667 = -0.0210 < 0\). The sign changes, so the root lies between \(2.2\) and \(2.3\) (it is \(x \approx 2.279\)).

book_ref.quote: The exact values can be refined using numerical methods

blocks.prompt: 29 Using graphs, explain why \(2\sin x = 3\) has no solution.
blocks.explanation: The equation is \(\sin x = \frac{3}{2}\). The graph \(y = \sin x\) lies between \(y = -1\) and \(y = 1\), while \(y = \frac{3}{2}\) is a horizontal line above it. They never intersect, so there is no solution.

book_ref.quote: Each point where the curves intersect represents a solution to the equation.

blocks.prompt: 30 A tower 25 m high stands on level ground. Find the angle of elevation of its top from a point \(25\sqrt{3}\) m from its foot.
blocks.explanation: \(\tan\theta = \frac{25}{25\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \Rightarrow \theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = 30^{\circ}\).

book_ref.quote: In each right triangle write

blocks.prompt: 31 The angle of elevation of the top of a pole from a point 15 m from its foot is \(45^{\circ}\). Find the height of the pole.
blocks.explanation: \(\tan 45^{\circ} = \frac{h}{15} \Rightarrow h = 15 \times 1 = 15\) m.

book_ref.quote: an angle at the observer is \(\tan^{-1}\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}\)

blocks.prompt: 32 Write \(\tan^{-1}3 - \tan^{-1}1\) as a single inverse tangent.

book_ref.quote: turns the difference into one inverse tangent

blocks.prompt: 33 A stone is thrown with \(v_0 = 20\) m/s. Using \(R = \frac{v_0^{2}}{g}\sin 2\theta\) with \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\), find the maximum range and the angle that gives it.
blocks.explanation: \(R\) is largest when \(\sin 2\theta = 1\), i.e. \(\theta = 45^{\circ}\). \(R_{\max} = \frac{400}{9.8} \approx 40.82\) m.

book_ref.quote: The range is maximized when \(\sin 2\theta\) is maximized.

blocks.prompt: 34 Show that the launch angles \(\theta\) and \(90^{\circ} - \theta\) give the same range \(R = \frac{v_0^{2}}{g}\sin 2\theta\).
blocks.explanation: For \(90^{\circ} - \theta\): \(\sin 2(90^{\circ} - \theta) = \sin(180^{\circ} - 2\theta) = \sin 2\theta\). So \(R\) is the same for both angles.

book_ref.quote: Complementary launch angles always give the same range

blocks.prompt: 35 Find the range of a ball thrown at \(30^{\circ}\) with \(v_0 = 14\) m/s (\(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\)), using \(R = \frac{v_0^{2}}{g}\sin 2\theta\).
blocks.explanation: \(R = \frac{196}{9.8}\sin 60^{\circ} = 20 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 10\sqrt{3} \approx 17.32\) m.

book_ref.quote: keep only the answers that make physical sense

blocks.prompt: 36 A 5 m flagpole stands on top of a 20 m building. Find the angle the flagpole subtends at a point on the ground 20 m from the foot of the building.
blocks.explanation: Subtract the angle to the foot of the flagpole from the angle to its top.

book_ref.quote: The angle an object subtends (between the lines to its bottom and its top) is a difference of two such angles.

steps: Angle to the top: \(\tan^{-1}\frac{25}{20} = \tan^{-1}\frac{5}{4}\); angle to the foot of the pole: \(\tan^{-1}\frac{20}{20} = \tan^{-1}1\)

blocks.prompt: 37 A 10 m ladder leans against a vertical wall and reaches 8 m up the wall. Find the angle the ladder makes with the ground.
blocks.explanation: \(\sin\theta = \frac{8}{10} = 0.8 \Rightarrow \theta = \sin^{-1}0.8 \approx 53.13^{\circ}\) (an acute angle, as it must be).

book_ref.quote: gives the angle in \([-90^{\circ}, 90^{\circ}]\) whose sine is

blocks.prompt: 38 With \(v_0 = 20\) m/s and \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\), can a projectile reach a target (i) 30 m away (ii) 50 m away? Use \(R = \frac{v_0^{2}}{g}\sin 2\theta\).
blocks.explanation: (i) \(\sin 2\theta = \frac{30 \times 9.8}{400} = 0.735\), which is between 0 and 1: yes. (ii) \(\sin 2\theta = \frac{50 \times 9.8}{400} = 1.225 > 1\): impossible, so the target cannot be reached (\(R_{\max} \approx 40.82\) m).

book_ref.quote: The value is between 0 and 1, so solutions exist.
